newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong movie chiefs say no fear of China censor.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong movie chiefs say no fear of China censor.

text.p: In three weeks, the world's third largest movie industry joins a country that censors all films, but Hong Kong is confident its free-wheeling studios will thrive beyond the handover to China.

With martial-arts stars like Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan, Hong Kong studios have thrilled cinemagoers around the globe for decades. The territory lags behind only Hollywood and Bombay as a movie producer, and is the world's second largest movie exporter.
On July 1, those studios will enter a new era when the British colony reverts to China, which keeps studios on a tight leash and allows only a selected handful of foreign movies to be imported.
But Hong Kong studio owners and government authorities promised that China's leash will not extend into the territory.

"There is no question of our operating under the direction of the central government at all in respect of the film and television industries," Chau Tak-hay, Secretary for Broadcasting, Culture and Sport, said on Wednesday.

Speaking at the opening of the Hong Kong International Film Market, Chau said China's promise of "one country, two systems" meant Hong Kong would police its own movies and broadcasts, and that meant only enforcing local standards on sex and violence.
"Beyond that we have no other criteria to say which films or which TV programmes may or may not be shown," he said. "No political criteria, and that will continue to be the case."
China's record on censorship is mixed. Chinese films by directors such as Zhang Yimou have pushed into previously taboo areas and won international applause in recent years.

But when Zhang was deemed too critical, Chinese censors refused to let his movies be shown at international film festivals, and ordered him to work only in China, where money is scarce and technology backward.

Even Hong Kong movies are not entirely exempt. When local director Cheung Yuen-ting finished her film on the Soong sisters, who played pivotal roles during China's early revolutionary period, she was amazed to find censors waving scissors.
"They cut two major scenes that did a lot of harm to the balance of the picture," Cheung said in a recent interview.
Beijing's censors could cut the Hong Kong production because it was made in China about famous Chinese personalities, which meant it required approval from the official film bureau.
But studio boss Raymond Chow of Golden Harvest, who brought the world Bruce Lee, said censorship existed throughout the world, and there was no need to worry excessively about China.
While "one country, two systems" offered protection for Hong Kong's way of doing business, Chow said the handover also offered the prospect of "one country, one great film industry".

"In production, distribution or exhibition, it will be much easier to get talent and manpower," Chow said. "And on the other end, with the gradual opening up of China, it will become the world's most important consumer market for film entertainment."

But Hong Kong studio bosses have more pressing worries than any possibility of Chinese censors -- Hollywood is muscling in on their home turf. While local productions used to outdraw imports three to one in local theaters, now they are about even.
